newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE-Evangelicals threaten Inca traditions in Peru.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Evangelicals threaten Inca traditions in Peru.

text.p: Wearing a wide-brimmed felt hat to protect himself from the sun, Santos Gallindo straddles a stream flowing from the rock face and offers incantations to the Inca deity Pachamama, Mother Earth.

"We trust in you Pachamama to protect our animals as they come down from the mountains for winter," he intones in his native Quechua language. "Accept these gifts of fruit, potatoes and corn spirit as a sign of respect and thanks."

As mayor of Quispillacta, a town perched high on the sides of the Pampa river valley, it is Gallindo's role to continue a tradition his forefathers have carried out since pre-Hispanic times. But the rise of the Evangelical church, with its purist theological line, is threatening the future of this throwback to the Inca age.

"We won't have any part in these goings-on. The Bible clearly bans all forms of idol worshipping," Alejandro Nunez, pastor of Quispillacta's Assembly of God church, said, thumbing through the good book for a passage to back up his claim. "I've banned the traditional festivals this year because they don't reflect the word of God."

This is a potent gesture as up to eighty percent of this village in the remote central highland region of Ayacucho belongs to the Evangelical church. There have been Protestant sects across South America since the early 1800s but the Evangelical church made slow progress in Peru until the Maoist Shining Path began its guerrilla activities in 1980.
EVANGELICALS THRIVE IN REMOTE AREAS

As the Catholic church retreated from rural areas during the troubles, the Evangelicals' dedication to finding new converts meant they stubbornly stayed and thrived as the only grassroots religious outlet for the population. With their forthright style of conversion, which has been controversial and often criticised, they have been especially successful in isolated jungle and mountain areas.

Their commitment has paid dividends. Fifteen years ago just three per cent of the population of Ayacucho professed to be Evangelicals. Now, Ayacucho University anthropologist Geoffrey Gammala says, the figure is 22 per cent. Nationwide, there are 2.5 million Evangelical worshippers in a total population of 24 million.

The survival of Inca traditions owes much to the plethora of religions that confronted Spanish clerics accompanying the 16th century conquistadores. While the Incas had a highly centralized administration, each ethnic group within their kingdom maintained its own deities and customs. Realising that it was impossible to extinguish all forms of Andean beliefs, the Catholics started a process of mutual adaptation, melding Catholic and traditional beliefs.

One of the many religious hybrids this tolerance produced is Quispillacta's festival of the Virgin of Carmen who, although nominally a Catholic saint, is also deemed to be an incarnation of the Inca Earth god, Machamama. It is said that if at festival time the Virgin is judged to look sad the harvest will be poor, if happy it will be bountiful.
CULTURE ROOTED IN ANDEAN BELIEFS

"Our culture in Peru has its roots in Andean beliefs," Monsignor Salvador Carvero, archdeacon of Ayacucho cathedral, said. "For the rural Peruvian the Catholic church has realised the need to find a middle ground between the Vatican and the condor or mountain worshipping ceremonies of the Andes."
He reserves his vitriol for the new sects: "The evangelicals are fanatical. All they know is how to quote the Bible without any appreciation of Peruvian culture."

Anthropologists such as Gammala are concerned not so much with the purely religious aspect of the cultural change but that it is causing social conflicts. "This is potentially devastating within fragile communities recovering after the years of terrorism," he says.

As head of one of Quispillactas' "Ayllus," the smallest traditional rural unit of six families, it is an aspect of the religious split that Tito Achalma has seen first hand. "The four Evangelical families practically shun the other two, some even refuse to work together at harvest time," he said.

In spite of the obvious problems caused by the Evangelicals' hard religious line, most new converts seem to be of one voice in saying that this is a small price to pay for religious purity and following the letter of the Bible.
'WHAT KIND OF RELIGION IS THAT?'

At the daily Assembly of God service in a thatched chapel, near where Shining Path guerrillas started their armed struggle by burning ballot boxes in the town hall of the adjoining village of Chuschi, church treasurer Jerardo Wamani has no regrets. "At festival time the Catholics get drunk on chicha (an Andean drink distilled from corn). They dance, sing and worship idols. Just what kind of religion is that?"
Quispillacta's increasingly small band of Catholics say they will celebrate as usual this year. "They can't stop us from worshipping," a defiant Tito Achalma said. "You just come along and watch us!"

Mayor Gallindo, however, remains more circumspect about the future. "There will come a time when no festivals are held at all. It's sad. The link our descendants had with the natural world around them is being broken."

Over a glass of chicha in Quispillacta's one remaining bar, Tito Achalma admits that until a year ago he too was an Evangelical. What caused him to go back to the Catholic fold? Apart from the desire to carry on traditional customs, he admits to a far more earthly motivation. The prospect of a lifetime without the odd glass of chicha was worth the risk of possible eternal damnation.
